f1: Hydrogen makes up about three-quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe by mass, and it fuels every shining star.
f2: Henry Cavendish identified it in 1766; Lavoisier named it 'water-former' because it burns to make water.

f1: Helium was discovered in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, decades before anyone found it on Earth.
f2: Earth's helium builds up underground from radioactive decay of uranium and thorium, and is extracted from natural gas.

f1: Lithium is the lightest metal, so light that it floats on water while fizzing as it reacts.
f2: Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries power phones, laptops and electric cars.

f1: Beryllium is almost transparent to X-rays, so it is used for the windows of X-ray tubes and detectors.
f2: Emeralds and aquamarines are both forms of beryl, a beryllium aluminum silicate mineral.

f1: Boron is the secret of borosilicate glass, such as Pyrex, which survives sudden heating and cooling without cracking.
f2: Boron carbide is one of the hardest materials known and is used in body armor.

f1: Carbon's knack for forming endless chains and rings makes it the backbone of every known living thing.
f2: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon; only the arrangement of their atoms differs.

f1: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air you breathe, yet most living things cannot use it directly.
f2: The Haber–Bosch process turns air's nitrogen into ammonia, making the fertilizer that feeds billions of people.

f1: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass, mostly locked up in rocks as silicates and oxides.
f2: The oxygen in our air was released by photosynthesis, starting with ancient bacteria over two billion years ago.

f1: Fluorine is the most reactive element of all, combining with almost everything, even the supposedly inert gas xenon.
f2: Fluoride in toothpaste and drinking water strengthens tooth enamel against decay.

f1: Neon glows a vivid reddish-orange when electricity passes through it, the classic color of neon signs.
f2: Many other 'neon' sign colors actually come from different gases or from coatings inside the tubes.

f1: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, yet combined with chlorine it becomes ordinary table salt.
f2: It is soft enough to cut with a knife, revealing a shiny surface that tarnishes within moments.

f1: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light, once used for photographic flashes and still used in flares and fireworks.
f2: A magnesium atom sits at the heart of every chlorophyll molecule, helping plants capture sunlight.

f1: Before cheap smelting arrived in 1886, aluminum was a precious metal, prized enough to cap the Washington Monument.
f2: It is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, but almost never occurs naturally as pure metal.

f1: Silicon is the heart of modern electronics: nearly every computer chip is built on an ultra-pure silicon wafer.
f2: It is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, mostly locked in sand and silicate rocks.

f1: Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand, who boiled down huge quantities of urine searching for the philosopher's stone.
f2: White phosphorus glows faintly in the dark as it slowly reacts with oxygen in the air.

f1: Sulfur, the 'brimstone' of old, forms bright yellow crystals around volcanic vents and hot springs.
f2: Sulfur compounds are behind the smells of rotten eggs, skunk spray and garlic.

f1: Chlorine gas was a deadly weapon in World War I, yet chlorine disinfection now keeps much of the world's drinking water safe.
f2: It is a yellow-green gas, and its name comes from the Greek for 'pale green'.

f1: Argon is the third most abundant gas in Earth's air, at almost 1 percent, far more than carbon dioxide.
f2: Its name comes from the Greek for 'lazy', because it reacts with almost nothing.

f1: Potassium is so reactive that it bursts into a lilac-colored flame when dropped into water.
f2: Humphry Davy isolated it in 1807, the first metal ever isolated by electrolysis.

f1: Calcium is the most abundant metal in the human body, mostly stored in bones and teeth.
f2: Limestone, marble and chalk are all calcium carbonate, much of it from the shells of ancient sea creatures.

f1: Mendeleev predicted scandium in 1871 as 'eka-boron', and when it was found in 1879, it closely matched his forecast.
f2: Lars Fredrik Nilson discovered it in Sweden and named it after Scandinavia.

f1: Titanium is as strong as many steels but around 45 percent lighter, making it prized for aircraft and spacecraft.
f2: The body tolerates titanium well, so it is used for hip replacements and dental implants.

f1: Vanadium is named after Vanadís, a Norse goddess of beauty, because its compounds come in so many vivid colors.
f2: A little vanadium makes steel tough and shock-resistant, ideal for tools and springs.

f1: Chromium gives rubies their red and emeralds their green; the color depends on the crystal surrounding it.
f2: Stainless steel stays shiny because its chromium forms an invisible, self-repairing oxide layer.

f1: Most mined manganese, around 90 percent, goes into making iron and steel, where it adds strength and toughness.
f2: Vast fields of manganese-rich nodules lie scattered across the deep ocean floor.

f1: Iron is the most abundant element in Earth as a whole by mass, mostly concentrated in the planet's core.
f2: Iron in hemoglobin carries oxygen around your body and helps give blood its red color.

f1: Cobalt is named after kobolds, mischievous goblins that German miners blamed for troublesome ores that gave off poisonous fumes.
f2: Cobalt compounds have colored glass and ceramics a deep 'cobalt blue' for thousands of years.

f1: Nickel's name comes from 'Kupfernickel', or 'Old Nick's copper', an ore that German miners thought was bewitched copper.
f2: Most nickel goes into stainless steel, where it adds toughness and corrosion resistance.

f1: Copper was one of the first metals humans used, worked into ornaments and tools more than 9,000 years ago.
f2: It conducts electricity better than any metal except silver, so it wires our homes and devices.

f1: Zinc coatings protect steel from rust by corroding first, sacrificing themselves to save the iron beneath.
f2: Brass, used in musical instruments and fittings, is an alloy of copper and zinc.

f1: Gallium melts at about 30 °C, so a solid piece will melt in the warmth of your hand.
f2: Mendeleev predicted it as 'eka-aluminum'; Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered it in 1875.

f1: The first transistor, built at Bell Labs in 1947, was made of germanium, before silicon took over electronics.
f2: Mendeleev predicted it as 'eka-silicon'; Clemens Winkler found it in 1886 and named it after Germany.

f1: Arsenic was so popular with poisoners that it earned the grim nickname 'inheritance powder'.
f2: The Marsh test, devised in 1836, gave forensic scientists a reliable way to detect arsenic.

f1: Selenium conducts electricity better in light than in darkness, a discovery that led to early light meters and photocopiers.
f2: Jöns Jacob Berzelius discovered it in 1817 and named it after Selene, the Greek moon goddess.

f1: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury.
f2: It is a dark red-brown liquid with choking fumes; its name comes from the Greek for 'stench'.

f1: From 1960 to 1983, the meter was officially defined by the orange-red light given off by krypton-86 atoms.
f2: Ramsay and Travers discovered it in 1898; its name comes from the Greek 'kryptos', meaning hidden.

f1: Rubidium atoms tick inside compact atomic clocks used in GPS satellites and telecommunications networks.
f2: Bunsen and Kirchhoff discovered it in 1861 by spotting deep red lines in a mineral's spectrum.

f1: Strontium salts give fireworks and emergency flares their brilliant crimson red color.
f2: It is named after Strontian, a Scottish village where its mineral was first found.

f1: Yttrium is one of four elements named after Ytterby, a single small mining village in Sweden.
f2: Johan Gadolin identified its oxide in 1794 from a black mineral found near Ytterby.

f1: Zirconium barely absorbs neutrons, so it sheathes the uranium fuel inside most nuclear reactors.
f2: Zircon grains about 4.4 billion years old from Western Australia are among the oldest known Earth minerals.

f1: Niobium–titanium wire forms the superconducting magnets in most MRI scanners and in the Large Hadron Collider.
f2: It is named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, because it is so chemically similar to tantalum.

f1: Molybdenum melts at about 2,620 °C, and adding it to steel helps the steel stay strong when red-hot.
f2: Its name comes from the Greek for lead, because its ore was long confused with lead ore and graphite.

f1: Technetium was the first element made artificially, and its name comes from the Greek word for 'artificial'.
f2: Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè found it in 1937 in molybdenum bombarded in a cyclotron.

f1: Ruthenium was the last platinum-group metal to be discovered, and it is named after Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia.
f2: Karl Ernst Claus isolated it in 1844 at Kazan University from platinum ore residues.

f1: Rhodium is one of the rarest and most expensive precious metals, vital to catalytic converters that clean car exhaust.
f2: Its name comes from the Greek 'rhodon', meaning rose, after the color of its salts.

f1: Palladium can soak up around 900 times its own volume of hydrogen gas, like a metal sponge.
f2: Wollaston discovered it in 1803 and named it after the asteroid Pallas, found the year before.

f1: Silver is the best electrical conductor of all the elements and reflects more visible light than any other metal.
f2: Light-sensitive silver halide crystals made film photography possible.

f1: Cadmium yellows and reds are brilliant, long-lasting artists' pigments, popular with painters since the 19th century.
f2: Friedrich Stromeyer discovered it in 1817 as an impurity in zinc carbonate.

f1: Indium tin oxide is a transparent conductor of electricity, which makes touchscreens and flat-panel displays possible.
f2: It was discovered in 1863 and named for the bright indigo line in its spectrum.

f1: Bending a bar of tin makes an eerie crackling sound, called 'tin cry', as its crystals slip and twin.
f2: Combined with copper, tin makes bronze, the alloy that gave the Bronze Age its name.

f1: Antimony sulfide was used as black eye makeup in the ancient world, giving antimony its symbol, Sb, from 'stibium'.
f2: Antimony compounds are widely used as flame retardants in plastics, textiles and electronics.

f1: Absorbing even a tiny amount of tellurium can give a person garlicky 'tellurium breath' that lingers for weeks.
f2: Its name comes from 'tellus', the Latin word for Earth.

f1: When warmed, iodine's dark crystals give off a striking violet vapor, which inspired its name, from the Greek for violet.
f2: Bernard Courtois discovered it in 1811 while extracting chemicals for gunpowder from seaweed ash.

f1: Xenon was the first noble gas made to form a chemical compound, in 1962, overturning the belief that these gases were inert.
f2: It makes up only about 90 parts per billion of Earth's air.

f1: The second is officially defined by cesium-133 atoms: exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles of a microwave frequency characteristic of the atom.
f2: It melts at about 28 °C, so it can turn liquid on a hot day.

f1: Patients drink a barium sulfate 'milkshake' so their digestive tract shows up clearly on X-rays.
f2: Barium sulfate is safe because it barely dissolves, but soluble barium compounds are poisonous.

f1: Lanthanum gives its name to the lanthanides, the 15 metals running from lanthanum to lutetium.
f2: Its name comes from the Greek for 'to lie hidden', as it hid in cerium minerals.

f1: Cerium is the most abundant rare earth element, and scraping its iron alloy produces the sparks in lighter flints.
f2: It was named after the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier in 1801.

f1: Praseodymium means 'green twin': it was split from 'didymium', a substance once thought to be a single element.
f2: Carl Auer von Welsbach separated didymium into praseodymium and neodymium in 1885.

f1: Neodymium magnets are the strongest widely available permanent magnets, packing a powerful pull into tiny sizes.
f2: They are found in headphones, hard drives, electric car motors and wind turbines.

f1: Promethium has no stable isotopes, making it one of only two elements lighter than lead that are entirely radioactive.
f2: It was confirmed in 1945 at Oak Ridge, among the products of uranium fission.

f1: Samarium was the first element named, indirectly, after a person: Russian mining official Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets.
f2: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated it in 1879 from the mineral samarskite.

f1: Europium, named after Europe, glows red or blue under ultraviolet light and helps color many screens and lamps.
f2: Eugène-Anatole Demarçay isolated it in 1901.

f1: Gadolinium compounds are injected as MRI contrast agents to make blood vessels and tumors stand out.
f2: It is magnetic only below about 20 °C, so a chilly room can switch its magnetism on.

f1: Terbium compounds glow bright green under ultraviolet light and supply the green in many fluorescent lamps and screens.
f2: It is one of four elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.

f1: Dysprosium's name comes from the Greek for 'hard to get at', after years of difficult separation work.
f2: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran identified it in 1886.

f1: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element, so it helps concentrate the fields of the strongest magnets.
f2: It is named after Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm.

f1: Erbium-doped fibers amplify the light signals that carry internet traffic through undersea cables.
f2: It is one of four elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.

f1: Thulium is named after Thule, a legendary land in the far north often linked with Scandinavia.
f2: Per Teodor Cleve discovered it in 1879.

f1: Ytterbium atoms power some of the most precise optical atomic clocks ever built.
f2: It is one of four elements named after the Swedish village of Ytterby.

f1: Lutetium, the last of the lanthanides, was named after Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.
f2: Georges Urbain, Carl Auer von Welsbach and Charles James separated it independently around 1907.

f1: Hafnium hid inside zirconium minerals for over a century, because the two elements are almost chemically identical.
f2: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy discovered it in 1923, naming it after Hafnia, Latin for Copenhagen.

f1: Tantalum capacitors pack a lot of electrical storage into tiny spaces, making them common in phones and laptops.
f2: Anders Gustaf Ekeberg discovered it in 1802 and named it after Tantalus of Greek myth.

f1: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,420 °C, which is why it glowed in old light bulbs.
f2: Its symbol, W, comes from 'wolfram', an old name linked to its ore, wolframite.

f1: Rhenium, found in 1925, was the last stable element to be discovered.
f2: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg discovered it and named it after the Rhine River.

f1: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, about twice as dense as lead.
f2: Its name comes from the Greek 'osme', meaning smell, after the pungent odor of its oxide.

f1: A worldwide layer of iridium-rich clay marks the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs, 66 million years ago.
f2: It is the most corrosion-resistant metal known.

f1: Spanish colonists in South America called platinum 'platina', little silver, and often saw it as a nuisance in gold mining.
f2: Catalytic converters use platinum to turn harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.

f1: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be hammered into a sheet about one square meter in area.
f2: Gold barely reacts with anything, which is why ancient gold artifacts still gleam today.

f1: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and it was once called quicksilver.
f2: Its symbol, Hg, comes from 'hydrargyrum', meaning 'water-silver'.

f1: Thallium was nicknamed 'the poisoner's poison' because its salts are tasteless, odorless and deadly.
f2: William Crookes discovered it in 1861 by spotting a bright green line in a spectrum.

f1: Romans made water pipes from lead, and the word 'plumbing' comes from its Latin name, plumbum, also the source of Pb.
f2: Lead is toxic, especially to children's developing brains, so leaded gasoline and lead paint were phased out.

f1: Bismuth was found to be radioactive in 2003, but its half-life is over a billion times the age of the universe.
f2: Bismuth crystals grow in stepped, staircase shapes, with rainbow colors from a thin oxide film.

f1: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered polonium in 1898 and named it after Marie's homeland, Poland.
f2: Polonium-210 is so intensely radioactive that a small sample heats itself to hundreds of degrees Celsius.

f1: Astatine is so rare and so radioactive that no one has ever seen a visible sample of it.
f2: It was first made in 1940 at Berkeley by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles.

f1: Radon, a radioactive gas seeping from rocks and soil, is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
f2: It is colorless and odorless, so homes in risk areas are checked with simple detectors.

f1: Francium is so unstable that its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of only about 22 minutes.
f2: Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939 at the Curie Institute and named it after France.

f1: Radium paint made watch dials glow, but many 'Radium Girls' who applied it later suffered and died from radiation poisoning.
f2: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered it in 1898, later extracting it from tons of pitchblende ore.

f1: Actinium glows a pale blue in the dark, because its intense radioactivity excites the surrounding air.
f2: André-Louis Debierne discovered it in 1899 in residues of pitchblende left after the Curies' work.

f1: Thorium is three to four times more abundant in Earth's crust than uranium, and it could one day fuel nuclear reactors.
f2: Jöns Jacob Berzelius discovered it in 1829 and named it after Thor, Norse god of thunder.

f1: Protactinium's name means 'before actinium', because it decays into actinium.
f2: Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner identified its longest-lived isotope, protactinium-231, in 1917–18.

f1: A uranium nucleus can split in two; that fission, discovered in 1938, powers nuclear reactors and atomic weapons.
f2: Martin Heinrich Klaproth discovered it in 1789 and named it after the recently found planet Uranus.

f1: Neptunium was the first element heavier than uranium ever made, and is named after Neptune, the planet beyond Uranus.
f2: Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson produced it at Berkeley in 1940 by bombarding uranium with neutrons.

f1: Plutonium-238 gives off so much heat that it powers deep-space probes like Voyager and Mars rovers like Curiosity.
f2: Glenn Seaborg's team first made it at Berkeley in 1940–41.

f1: A tiny speck of americium-241 sits inside many household smoke detectors, ionizing air so smoke can be sensed.
f2: Glenn Seaborg's team identified it in 1944 at the University of Chicago's wartime Metallurgical Laboratory.

f1: Curium is named after Marie and Pierre Curie, pioneers in the study of radioactivity.
f2: Seaborg, Ralph James and Albert Ghiorso first made it in 1944 by bombarding plutonium with alpha particles.

f1: Berkelium is named after Berkeley, California, where it was first made in 1949.
f2: Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso and Glenn Seaborg made it by bombarding americium with alpha particles.

f1: Californium-252 gives off so many neutrons that tiny amounts are used to start nuclear reactors and probe rocks in oil wells.
f2: It was first made at Berkeley in 1950 and named after the state of California.

f1: Einsteinium was first found in debris from the first full-scale hydrogen bomb test, 'Ivy Mike', in 1952.
f2: Its discovery was kept secret for several years because of Cold War security.

f1: Fermium is the heaviest element that can be built up by bombarding lighter elements with neutrons.
f2: It was first identified, alongside einsteinium, in debris from the 1952 'Ivy Mike' hydrogen bomb test.

f1: Mendelevium was first made in 1955 literally one atom at a time: just 17 atoms in the original experiments.
f2: It is named after Dmitri Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table.

f1: Nobelium is named after Alfred Nobel, but its discovery was hotly disputed by laboratories in Sweden, the US and the USSR.
f2: The name came from a 1957 claim made in Stockholm that later proved to be wrong.

f1: Lawrencium, named after cyclotron inventor Ernest Lawrence, is the last member of the actinide series.
f2: Albert Ghiorso's team at Berkeley first reported it in 1961 by bombarding californium with boron.

f1: Rutherfordium, the first element beyond the actinides, is named after Ernest Rutherford, a founding father of nuclear physics.
f2: Soviet and American teams both claimed it, in 1964 and 1969, and proposed different names.

f1: Dubnium is named after Dubna, the Russian science town where much of the hunt for superheavy elements has taken place.
f2: It was reported by Dubna in 1968 and by Berkeley in 1970, sparking a long naming dispute.

f1: Seaborgium was the first element named after a person who was still alive: American chemist Glenn T. Seaborg.
f2: It was first made at Berkeley in 1974 by bombarding californium with oxygen ions.

f1: Bohrium is named after Niels Bohr, whose model of the atom helped launch quantum physics.
f2: A team at the GSI laboratory in Darmstadt, Germany, first convincingly made it in 1981.

f1: Hassium is named after the German state of Hesse, home of the GSI laboratory where it was first made in 1984.
f2: It was made by fusing iron nuclei with lead.

f1: Meitnerium honors Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission but was left out of the Nobel Prize for it.
f2: A team at GSI in Darmstadt first detected a single atom of it in 1982.

f1: Darmstadtium is named after Darmstadt, Germany, where GSI scientists first made it in 1994.
f2: It was made by fusing nickel nuclei with lead.

f1: Roentgenium is named after Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays in 1895.
f2: GSI scientists first made three atoms of it in 1994 by fusing nickel and bismuth.

f1: Copernicium, named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, behaves in single-atom experiments like a volatile relative of mercury.
f2: GSI scientists first made it in 1996 by fusing zinc and lead nuclei.

f1: Nihonium was the first element discovered in Asia; Japan's RIKEN team spent nine years collecting just three atoms.
f2: Its name comes from 'Nihon', one of the Japanese names for Japan.

f1: Flerovium was first made at Dubna, Russia, in 1998, and honors physicist Georgy Flyorov, founder of its laboratory.
f2: It was made by fusing calcium-48 with plutonium.

f1: Moscovium is named after the Moscow region, home of Dubna, where it was first made in 2003.
f2: A Russian–American team made it by firing calcium-48 nuclei at americium.

f1: Livermorium honors Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, whose scientists helped a Russian team make it.
f2: It was first made at Dubna in 2000 by fusing calcium-48 with curium.

f1: Making tennessine required rare berkelium from a Tennessee reactor, flown to Russia and bombarded with calcium ions.
f2: A Russian–American collaboration first reported it in 2010.

f1: Oganesson, element 118, completes the periodic table's seventh row, and only a handful of its atoms have ever been detected.
f2: It is only the second element named after a living person, nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian.
